results.active_slot_saturation: 65th distinct set rejected; same-key leases coalesce; only a retired idle entry can be evicted. Unfinished aborted work retains its slot until completion.
results.background_ownership: Final public clone cancels pending acquisition and refresh; a surviving clone or caller preserves work. Cached connection-open managers use demand acquisition and create no refresh timers.
results.credential_isolation: Length/presence-delimited SHA-256 includes all credential and TLS field roles; no raw configuration strings remain in keys.
results.strict_lint: Stable all targets/all features and focused Rust 1.85 all-feature checks passed.

first_failures.development_lifecycle_race: Expiry/refresh interleaving initially dropped an acquisition result. Separating retirement epochs from token refresh epochs fixed it; all four final matrices passed.
first_failures.development_compile_and_lint: Unused-result, Send-bound, and unfulfilled lint-expectation failures are retained.
first_failures.documentation_checker_setup: First checker run lacked Rust on PATH; corrected setup passes all 18 tests.
first_failures.initial_peer_dependencies: Initial probe resolved tokio-rustls 0.26.6. It is preparation only; the four accepted runs use the copied repository lock with tokio-rustls 0.26.5.

limits: Local loopback HTTP/SASL peers and custom fetchers; no real identity provider, full Kafka broker, sustained soak, or production qualification.

Cache bounds cover retained manager count/config input and cache-owned acquisition slots. Caller-owned configurations, returned tokens, custom fetcher state, TLS internals and process RSS require their own budgets.
Idle credential/token retention is bounded by capacity rather than a TTL. New distinct sets can evict idle entries; temporary saturation or unfinished cancellation returns QueueFull.
Application-owned managers retain proactive refresh; the shared connect-time cache uses demand acquisition. Dropping an owner requests cancellation; tests observe completion on the running executor.
No throughput comparison, world-fastest claim, release, push, deployment or Suite HOLD change.
